correctness.rationale: The frozen proof did not establish all of its isolated-endpoint refinement: its nonnegative induction branch uses k=deg(u)+deg(v)<=1, which is sufficient but not necessary for isolation; when, for example, one endpoint is isolated and the other has degree two, its k>=2 branch proves only the universal lower bound. The statement itself remains true. The corrected files branch first on isolation regardless of k. For a fixed order, conditioning on its first edge proves the vertex-deletion difference is in {0,1}: if that edge avoids the deleted vertex, both take it and reduce to smaller graphs, and otherwise apply the smaller-graph induction to its other endpoint in the deleted graph. Under uniform order this gives the two-vertex deletion loss at most two, or at most one when one vertex is isolated. Subtracting the two first-edge recurrences gives (m+1)Delta = 1+mu(G-{u,v})-mu(G) plus the sum over q old edges disjoint from uv of the smaller differences. Isolation is inherited in every such summand; hence delta is nonnegative in the entire corrected branch. Otherwise k>=2 gives the lower numerator -1-q/3 >= -(m+1)/3; the upper numerator is at most 1+q. The empty graph and the four-vertex path formed from two disjoint edges attain +1 and -1/3 respectively.
residual_risks: Finite replay does not prove the universal statement; the corrected simultaneous induction does. The result concerns expected unweighted size, not pathwise lower damage -1/3.

evidence: The same-date wheel record proves under a fixed inherited order that deleting any vertex cannot increase greedy cardinality and can decrease it by at most one, even though the headline concerns cycle-to-wheel augmentation. The later leaf-augmentation result proves stochastic dominance for uniform decoration of all cores and analyzes a single-leaf coupling in that setting.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The wheel's general lemma genuinely covers the isolated-endpoint assertion: delete the formerly isolated endpoint from the augmented graph. Deleting either endpoint gives a common smaller graph and also the upper bound. Even for arbitrary fixed orders, deleting both endpoints gives only a loss bound of two; the sharp expectation lower bound needs random-order recurrence and is not supplied there.

checked_sources: Repaired RESULT.md, exact recurrence, induction and extremizers; same-date vertex-deletion comparison
value.rationale: An extra allowable match can make the randomized greedy policy worse, even though it cannot hurt the optimum. The repaired theorem quantifies exactly how bad one such change can be, by a graph-size-independent sharp constant stronger than the unit sensitivity from deleting vertices. The four-vertex example fixes the constant but is not the universal argument. This is a natural perturbation of a classical algorithm, not just a finite enumeration or a reformulation of the known deletion lemma.
residual_risks: No guarantee for weighted greedy matching, other order rules, multiple updates or individual random outcomes.
